To assess the performance of the warehouse simulation, this research employs a variety of indicators that are used to compare the impacts of different scenarios generated by the simulation process [25]. By utilizing these diverse parameters, the study aims to measure the extent to which each scenario can influence the operational performance of the warehouse. The selected parameters in the performance measurement criteria encompass several aspects directly related to the operational efficiency and productivity of the warehouse, which can be observed from the simulation outcomes. The details of the parameters used for evaluating warehouse performance are provided below.

Throughput is used to measure the number of orders that are successfully processed and completed within a specific period, compared to the number of orders that arrive in the system during the same period. It is an important parameter for evaluating the system's abil ity to manage and process orders efficiently. If throughput is low, it may indicate  the  bottlenecks  in  the  system,  which  may  require  process  improvement  or adjustments to enhance overall performance.

Robot utilization measures how frequently robots are used to perform tasks compared to the time they spend in idle. The higher the robot utilization rate, the more efficiently the system is using robots to carry out necessary tasks, meaning the robots are working optimally  with  minimal  wasted  time.  Conversely,  if  the  utilization  rate  is  low,  it indicates that robots spend a significant amount of time unused, which could suggest resource  wastage.  The  idle  time  not  only  wastes  the  robot's  capabilities  but  als o impacts overall operations by decreasing productivity and increasing costs.

The average order cycle time refers to the time required to process an order within the warehouse, starting  from  when  the  order  is  received  until  the  order  is  ready  to  be fulfilled. The speed at which each of these stages is completed significantly affects the total  order  cycle  time.  A  shorter  cycle  time  indicates  that  the  existing  warehouse management  system  operates  efficiently,  reducing  waiting  times  and  improving overall productivity. Conversely, a longer cycle may indicate issues in the workflow. If  these  issues  are  not  addressed  promptly,  they  can  not  only  affect  operational smoothness but also decrease customer satisfaction levels. Therefore, managing order cycle  time  effectively  is  crucial  as  it  can  optimize  warehouse  workflows,  reduce operational costs and ultimately speed up order completion time leading to improved company performance in the long run.

To evaluate the energy performance in warehouse simulations, this study adopts several indicators used to compare the impacts of different scenarios generated from the simulations [19].  The  evaluation  process  aims  to  provide  a  comprehensive  understanding  of  energy efficiency  within  the  operational  context  of  the  warehouse.  The  criteria  used  in  the performance measurement encompass various aspects related to energy efficiency, including specific parameters measured throughout the simulation process. By employing this approach, it is expected to gain a deeper understanding of the factors that influence energy usage in the warehouse and how changes in certain variables can impact overall energy performance.

Total  energy  consumption  refers  to  the  aggregate  amount  of  energy  expended  by robots  during  their  operational  processes.  A  lower  total  energy  consumption  is generally preferred, as it not only reflects reduced operational costs but also contributes to  minimizing  the  environmental  impact.  In  the  context  of  robot  routing,  elevated energy consumption may suggest the routing algorithm employed is suboptimal of inefficient in planning the robot's travel paths. By implementing more efficient routing methodology,  robots  can  minimize  the  distance  traveled  and  avoid  unnecessary movements, thereby leading to a reduction in overall energy consumption. Consequently, route optimal plays a crucial role in enhancing operational efficiency and mitigating energy use within robotic systems.

Energy per order refers to the average amount of energy used to process a single order within the system. This metric provides valuable information into the energy efficiency of the entire order fulfillment process. A lower energy per order value indicates a more efficient system, where energy consumption for processing each order is minimized, which in turn reduces  operational  costs  and  enhances  overall  performance.  On  the other hand, higher values suggest potential inefficiencies in the process, highlighting areas where improvements can be made to reduce energy consumption per order.

The number of starts and stops refers to the frequency with which robots initiate and halt their movements during operational tasks. A lower frequency of starts and stops is highly desirable, as it reflects smoother and more continuous operations, which not only  improve  energy  efficiency  but  also  reduce  wear  on  the  robot's  mechanical components. A more seamless operation, without excessive interruptions from starts and stops, can optimize energy consumption, minimize power wastage, and extend the lifespan o f the robot's components. In contrast, a higher frequency of starts and stops can lead to increased energy consumption, as the robot expends more power to start and stop its movements and accelerate the wear and tear on its moving parts.

Evaluating the performance of Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS) requires more than just assessing operational speed, it also involves careful consideration of energy efficiency  throughout  the  order  fulfillment  process.  Striking  an  effective  balance  between achieving  high  throughput  and  minimizing  energy  consumption  is  essential  for  reducing operational costs and promoting sustainability. A useful metric for evaluating this balance is throughput  efficiency  to  energy  per  order,  which  integrates  two  critical  performance dimensions into a single, comprehensive indicator that reflects both processing capacity and energy expenditure per order.

This metric facilitates the analysis of trade-offs between processing speed and energy usage, enabling more informed comparisons across various algorithmic approaches. It serves as an important benchmark  for determining which methods are most effective in simultaneously maximizing throughput while maintaining low energy consumption. In RMFS operations,  the  overarching  objective  is  to  enhance  efficiency  without  compromising environmental or economic considerations. To address the robot routing problem within this context,  this  study  adopts  a  hybrid  approach  that  integrates  the  A*  algorithm  with reinforcement learning using the QMIX framework . In this configuration, the A* algorithm is responsible for generating the initial path planning solution based on static map information, offering  reliable  and  efficient  routing.  Simultaneously,  the  QMIX  algorithm  enables  each autonomous robot to learn and adapt in real-time, refining its path to minimizing travel time and energy usage under dynamic warehouse conditions. By combining heuristic-based and learning-based strategies, the system can respond intelligently to environmental variability and operational demands. This hybrid framework not only improves the flexibility of robot motion planning but also supports more sustainable and cost-effective fulfillment operations. Therefore, selecting an appropriate algorithmic strategy must involve a holistic evaluation of both  performance  and  energy  impact,  with  the
goal  of  achieving  solutions  that  are  both operationally efficient and environmentally responsible.

Nevertheless, Energy per Order is minimized at 35 AMRs, demonstrating that the additional robots improve per-unit energy efficiency despite higher total energy demands. The Number of Starts and Stops increases proportionally with AMR count, while the trade-off metric achieves its highest value at 35 AMRs, confirming that the gains in throughput outweigh the associated energy costs.

headings: 4.4.3 Effect of Number of Picking Stations
chunks.text: The number of picking stations exerts a direct and positive influence on system throughput and order processing efficiency.  Throughput  is  highest  with  4  picking  stations,  followed  by  3 stations, and lowest with 2 stations, attributable to reduced bottlenecks at order transfer points and increased parallel processing capability. AOCT is minimized at 4 stations, reflecting the advantage of concurrent processing over sequential workflows. Robot utilization displays a slight decline with increasing station count, potentially due to a more balanced distribution of tasks and reduced congestion  in  robot  travel  paths.  Total  Energy  Consumption  increases  marginally  with  more picking  stations,  a  result  of  higher-frequency  but  shorter-distance  travel  cycles.  Nevertheless, Energy per Order is lowest at 4 stations, indicating that the system uses energy more effectively when processing throughput is maximized. The Number of Starts and Stops is positively correlated with the number of stations, while the trade-off metric peaks at 4 stations, confirming that the increase in throughput and per-unit energy efficiency outweighs the additional operational cycles.

The rapid growth of global e-commerce has intensified the need for innovative logistics and order  fulfillment  solutions,  especially  during  peak  order  surges  such  as  Black  Friday,  Cyber Monday,  and  holiday  seasons.  Customers  increasingly  expect  immediate  product  availability, competitive pricing, and expedited delivery. In response, many companies are investing in robotics and automation technologies, with Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS) emerging as a leading solution to enhance operational speed and picking efficiency. However, most prior studies remain focused on conventional optimization methods and have yet to fully explore intelligent and adaptive multi-robot coordination strategies.
This  study  addresses  this  gap  by  proposing  a  hybrid  approach  that  integrates  the  A* pathfinding algorithm with the QMIX algorithm, a state-of-the-art Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) method. This hybrid design leverages centralized training with decentralized execution to enable more efficient coordination among multiple agents operating in dynamic and large-scale warehouse environments.

Simulation results confirm that the proposed A* + QMIX algorithm significantly improves RMFS  performance  compared  to  the  A*  baseline  across  all  evaluated  metrics.  In  terms  of warehouse  performance,  the  average  throughput  increased  by  3.41  percentage  points,  from 89.191%  in  the  baseline  to  92.600%  in  the  proposed  approach.  This  improvement  was accompanied by a reduction in Average Order Cycle Time (AOCT) by 42 seconds (from 1,257 s to 1,215 s), indicating faster order completion. Robot utilization also improved from 99.50% to 99.85%, reflecting more optimal task allocation and reduced idle time.
From an energy perspective,  the  proposed  system  reduced  Total  Energy  Consumption  by 3.57% (from 73,234 kJ to 70,617 kJ) and lowered Energy per Order by 7.1% (from 48.3 kJ to 44.87 kJ). A contributing factor to this gain is the reduction in robot starts and stops by 9.83% (from  126,264  to  113,836),  minimizing  energy-intensive  stop-and-go  operations  and  reducing mechanical  wear.  Furthermore,  the  trade-off  ratio  between  throughput  and  energy  per  order

improved by 11.77%, from 1.847% in the baseline to 2.064% in the proposed method, confirming a better balance between productivity and energy efficiency.
Beyond performance evaluation, this research also conducted a sensitivity analysis on three critical operational parameters: order arrival rate, number of robots, and number of picking stations. The analysis  revealed  that  these  factors  have  a  substantial  and  varying  impact  on  throughput, AOCT, robot  utilization,  and  energy  consumption.  Notably,  an  order  arrival  rate  of  200 -225 orders/hour,  deployment  of  35  AMRs,  and  the  use  of  4  picking  stations  consistently  yielded optimal performance across most metrics. These findings provide actionable insights for strategic configuration and parameter tuning in real-world RMFS deployments.

Future  research  is  encouraged  to  develop  more  realistic  and  adaptive  RMFS  models  by extending the hybrid framework that combines the A* algorithm with the QMIX reinforcement learning approach. While this study demonstrates the potential of the hybrid method in enhancing both  pathfinding  accuracy  and  multi-agent  coordination,  the  current  implementation  operates under several simplifying assumptions, such as unlimited robot energy, static environment layouts, and  fixed  task  allocation.  To  provide  a  more  comprehensive  evaluation,  future  work  should incorporate  real-world  constraints  such  as  battery  depletion,  charging  station  logistics,  and operational costs.
Although QMIX effectively supports real-time learning and coordination among agents, and A* contributes to efficient path initialization, further research should explore how the integration between these two methods can be made more adaptive in dynamic and congested environments. This  includes  scenarios  involving  fluctuating  order  volumes,  real-time  task  prioritization,  and high-density  robot  traffic.  Developing  more  sophisticated  switching  mechanisms  or  hybrid policies  that  dynamically  balance  heuristic  and  learned  behaviors  could  enhance  system responsiveness under varying operational conditions.

In addition, conducting a Reward/α ablation study is recommended to analyze the effect of including energy terms in the reward function and varying the teamspirit parameter α. Such an analysis can provide deeper insights into how different reward configurations influence energy efficiency,  throughput,  and  overall  system  coordination,  thus  offering  guidance  for  optimal parameter tuning in diverse operational contexts.
Moreover, future studies may explore the incorporation of advanced reinforcement learning techniques, such as curiosity-driven learning or meta-learning, to improve the adaptability of the hybrid  model.  Comparative  analyses  between  hybrid  QMIX -A*  and  other  MARL-based frameworks,  including  IQL,  MADDPG,  or  MAPPO,  can  provide  deeper  insights  into  relative performance in RMFS contexts. Finally, the scalability of the hybrid framework should be assessed in large-scale deployments involving dozens or hundreds of AMRs. Investigating its computational efficiency, training stability, and convergence behavior in such settings is essential to ensure practical feasibility for real-world warehouse systems.
